scenario.title: SysTick period - off-by-one reload and a wrong clock assumption
scenario.description: A bare-metal program programs SysTick for a 1 ms tick and measures ten tick periods twice: with the core cycle counter (DWT CYCCNT) and with the 1 MHz system timer (TIMERAWL), which runs from its own reference and does not depend on the core clock. Three variants. "correct": RVR = 150000 - 1 for a 150 MHz core. "off_by_one": RVR = 150000, so every period is 150001 cycles. "wrong_clock": the reload is computed for 150 MHz, but the core is still running at 12 MHz (the clock setup was skipped), so each tick takes 12.5 times longer in real time while looking perfect in cycles.

variants.name: off_by_one
variants.hidden_symptom: A 1 ms software clock runs slightly slow: it lags by about half a second per day.

variants.name: wrong_clock
variants.hidden_symptom: The scheduler tick looks right when counted in CPU cycles, but on the scope every period is 12.5 times too long.

expected.summary: correct gives 150000 cycles and 1000 us per tick; off_by_one gives 150001 cycles per tick; wrong_clock gives 150000 cycles but 12500 us per tick.

scenario.what_to_look_for: The program times ticks 2 to 12, not 1 to 11: the first SysTick handler runs from a cold XIP cache and reads CYCCNT about 20 cycles later than the others, which would bias the result (a real effect worth seeing once: run "r2s run P16 --trace --kinds exception_entry,exception_return" and compare the first handler's duration with the second's). Then read the UART lines "10 ticks: cycles=" and "10 ticks: us=" in each variant, and summary.variants.<name>.tick (also in the measurements table). correct: 1500000 cycles and 10000 us. off_by_one: 1500010 cycles. One extra cycle at 150 MHz is about 6.7 ns per tick, 0.07 us over the 10 measured ticks, so the 1 MHz timer still reads 10000 us: invisible in a short test, but about 0.58 s per day at 1000 ticks per second. wrong_clock: 1500000 cycles (the cycle count cannot see the problem, it is counted in the wrong unit) but 125000 us. The irq_pend SysTick events are spaced 150000 or 150001 cycles apart; the t_us column of the trace uses the model's clock, so in wrong_clock the ticks are 12.5 ms apart.
likely_root_causes: RVR loaded with the period instead of period - 1: SysTick counts RVR..0, so the period is RVR + 1 cycles.
The reload computed for the final PLL frequency while the core still runs from the crystal or ring oscillator (clock setup skipped, failed, or done after SysTick setup).
CLKSOURCE (SYST_CSR bit 2) selecting the external reference instead of the processor clock, or the reverse, so the tick runs at a different rate than the formula assumes.
A reload larger than 24 bits (0xFFFFFF) silently truncated by the hardware.
how_to_debug: Time ten ticks with two independent clocks (CYCCNT and the 1 MHz timer, or a GPIO toggle on the scope). If cycles look right but time does not, the clock frequency is wrong; if both are off by a constant, the reload is wrong.
Read back SYST_RVR (0xE000E014) and SYST_CSR (0xE000E010) in GDB and redo the arithmetic: period = (RVR + 1) / f_clk.
Check the real core frequency: toggle a pin in a loop of known cycle count and measure it on the scope, or read the clock registers.
Convert every cycle measurement to time with the clock you measured, not the clock you intended.
scenario.what_this_means: A timer period is a count times a clock period, and both can be wrong independently. Counting in cycles confirms the count; only a second, independent time base confirms the clock. That is why the course asks for every on-chip number to be cross-checked on the oscilloscope.
scenario.hidden_symptom: The scheduler tick looks right in the debugger, but task periods measured on the scope are 12.5 times too long (or drift slowly).
